d.g: To say abruptly.

d.g: To eject or suddenly throw fluid or some other substance from a duct or other body structure.
To forcibly eject fluid from the urethra through sexual stimulation.
d.x: Men can ejaculate between 0.1 and 10 milliliters of semen on average.

ejaculate.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ē- Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *(H)ih₁kyeti Proto-Italic *jīkjō Proto-Italic *jakjōder. …

d.g: The uttering of a short, sudden exclamation or prayer, or the exclamation or prayer uttered.
The act of ejecting or suddenly throwing fluid or some other substance from a duct or other body structure.
A reflex in human beings and other mammals in response to sexual stimulation involving the forcible ejection from the urethra of, in males, semen; and, in females, vaginal fluid.
d.x: By repeating this process several times before ejaculation and by practicing this procedure, the man will learn to control his ejaculation.

ejaculation.e: From French éjaculation, borrowed from Latin ēiaculārī.

d.g: A person or thing that ejaculates.
A device that stimulates the sex organs of a male animal with electric impulses in order to extract semen from an animal.

ejaculator.e: English ejaculate English -or English ejaculator From ejaculate + -or.

d.g: The act of ejecting.
That which is ejected.
d.x: Volcanic ejection covered the village in ash.

ejection.e: From Middle French éjection, from Latin eiectio.

d.g: One who, or that which, ejects or dispossesses.
A jet jump for lifting water or withdrawing air from a space.
ejector seat: a pilot's seat in an airplane that can be forcibly ejected in the case of an emergency; then the pilot descends by parachute.
That part of the mechanism of a breech-loading firearm which ejects the empty shell.

ejector.e: English eject English -or English ejector From eject + -or.

d.g: To compel (a person or persons) to leave.
d.x: The man started a fight and was ejected from the bar.

d.g: To throw out or remove forcefully.
d.x: In other news, a Montreal man was ejected from his car when he was involved in an accident.

d.g: To compel (a sports player) to leave the field because of inappropriate behaviour.
To forcefully project oneself or another occupant from an aircraft (or, rarely, another type of vehicle), typically using an ejection seat or escape capsule.
d.x: The pilot lost control of the plane and had to eject.

eject.e: From Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus, perfect passive participle of ēiciō (“to throw out”), or from ēiectō, the frequentative form of the same verb, from ē-, combining form of ex (“out”), + iaciō (“to throw”).

d.g: A Mexican cooperative farm.
d.x: Ejidos are land-grant communities organized by the federal government. Each family has a plot, which cannot be sold and can only be inherited by one person. Each ejido member has a vote at ejido meetings.

ejido.e: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish ejido, from Latin exitus (“departure”), an early borrowing from Latin. Doublet of exit and exitus.

d.g: A canon of construction holding that when a general term follows a list of particular terms, the general term only applies to things similar to the particular terms. For example, in the list "sun, moon, and other large objects", the phrase "other large objects" only includes celestial bodies, not houses and elephants.
d.x: I would submit to the court that in order to determine the legislature's intent of the final phrase we need to apply the interpretive maxim of ejusdem generis to the sentence that contains the sequence.

ejusdem generis.e: From Latin ejusdem generis ("of the same kind").

d.g: US President Bill Clinton's admission that he had had an "improper physical relationship" with Monica Lewinsky.
d.x: And we now have a title to Clinton's speech to the nation last Monday night: The "Ejaculation Proclamation."

Ejaculation Proclamation.e: Rhyme with Emancipation Proclamation, a proclamation issued by US President Abraham Lincoln.

d.g: Premature ejaculation.
d.x: This can be done psychoanalytically, as for example in the suggestion that salt is a symbol of semen and that the objection to spilling it reflects an unconscious fear of ejaculatio praecox.

ejaculatio praecox.e: Modern Latin, from noun type formed from participle stem of Latin ējaculāri (“to eject”) + praecox (“early”).

d.g: The proportion of blood ejected out of the left ventricle with each heartbeat.
d.x: Isoproterenol produced vasodilatation and increased rate, with reduction of EDV and increase in ejection fraction in normal subjects.

ejuration.e: Borrowed from Latin ēiūrātiō, from ēiūrō (“to abjure, disown, resign”) + -tiō.
